ship.header: Captain's log, stardate 80234.8. The Ur-Dragon, version v1.0.0.
ship.situation: We put in at Tom Beloy's on the evening of Saturday the twenty-second of August, the first engagement of an evening that would run to two. Three vessels in the sector including our own: Alex flying a mono-red ship under Tannuk, Steadfast Second, and Tom flying Merfolk. We took our chair expecting a long game.
ship.narrative: On the second or third turn Alex resolved Blood Moon, and from that point the ship produced red and nothing else; every land we had laid that was not a basic answered to a Mountain instead. Smothering Tithe stayed in hand, as did every dragon that asked for more than one colour, and we were left with the red portion of the fleet and no other. What that portion could do, it did. Moltensteel Dragon came down late, and I paid sixteen life to enlarge it and struck Alex for twelve. If we were to be shut out of the game, I saw no reason to leave quietly.

assessment.text: The sixteen life was mine to spend and I spent it with the game already beyond recovery; I record it as a decision rather than an accident, and I would take it again in the same position.

The constraint is the supply of mana and not the selection of cards. Interaction, treasure, the cost discounts, haste and card draw are all in good order; they were simply unaffordable from the second turn onward, which is a fault of the supply line and not of the crew who man it.
Blood Moon is a hazard of sailing at this level, and some captains carry it. I do not intend to shape the ship around one card, and I do not enter the night as evidence that we need an answer to it.

orders.text: I have ordered Engineering to audit the mana base whole rather than in pieces: how many basic lands we carry and whether our land searches can come back empty, whether the sources we run answer what the dragons actually ask for rather than being serviceable in general, and what we give up in time each turn a land arrives tapped. Tapped lands are tolerable to a point, and I would like to know where that point is.

ship.coda: One colour and one dragon, and we used both. The record will show a defeat; it will also show that Alex finished the evening twelve lighter.

ship.header: Captain's log, stardate 80237.8. The Ur-Dragon, version v1.0.1.
ship.situation: We came alongside at Oliver's on the evening of Tuesday the twenty-fifth of August, the first engagement of two. Five vessels in the sector — Oliver, Ryan, Tom, Alex and ourselves — with our chair fourth in the order. This was the first sailing under the revised mana base, which had been laid in that same day.
ship.narrative: Engineering had raised the land count from thirty-one to thirty-six that morning, five aboard and five dragons ashore; my own reaction to the old figure was disbelief that we had ever sailed on it. It did not help. I returned one hand and kept the second — about three lands, a piece that would have made the dragons cheaper, and the commander, with Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm and further six-mana dragons behind them. The mana then failed to arrive: four and five lands on the sixth and seventh turns, three to five behind the rest of the table, while Alex was drawing on something near twelve as early as the fourth. The discount piece was removed before it could do its work. After that the board was established and cleared, established and cleared again. Something did assemble late, and it bought us some damage and some standing at the table. I did not close as a threat. I stayed out of the reckoning, let the other four reduce one another, and closed at the end.

assessment.text: I won this game by not being worth attacking, and I decline to enter it as a piloting achievement. It is also the shape of most of our recent wins, which is the part that gives me pause.

The ship did not win; the table's attrition won and we were the last standing. The shortfall in mana is not one night either — we have run three to five lands behind for four or five games now, and what it does downstream is that a piece sits in hand castable eventually, which announces the play a turn or two early and gives the table the time it needs to answer it. When the board comes down we take nothing from it.
The table carries a great deal of creature removal and clears the board often, and five vessels grinding one another down will leave somebody standing. Against a tighter table it will not be us.

orders.text: I have ordered Engineering to establish where the shortfall actually sits, given that thirty-six lands did not close it and that the deficit predates this night by four or five games.
I have ordered Ops to find what the ship recovers when the board is cleared, since at present it recovers nothing and the table clears it repeatedly.

ship.coda: The log records a win, and the log is correct. I would rather have earned it.

ship.header: Captain's log, stardate 80244.8. The Ur-Dragon, version v1.0.2.
ship.situation: The second engagement of three at Oliver's, taken up after we had flown goblin-storm in the first. The same five vessels in the sector: Oliver, Tom, Alex, Ryan and ourselves. This sailing was the first meant to test the work Engineering has been doing under measurement rather than impression — the first arrangement carried thirty-one lands and little else that made mana, the second added lands and access to colours, and this third shifted the weight toward creatures and artifacts that produce it.
ship.narrative: The mana worked. Engineering had four mana available on the first turn and five on the second, in a ship that asks for all five colours, and the fleet came down in order behind it. Then I played Gadrak, the Crown-Scourge a turn earlier than I should have, and in doing so told the table exactly what was coming: two copies of Terror of the Peaks and twenty damage aimed wherever I chose, twenty-eight in the air on the following swing. They converged as one. Tom took all three of our artifacts so that Gadrak, which requires four, could not be activated; Alex sent his creatures into the dragons; Ryan removed what was left; Tom finished the matter from across the table. We were taken apart before we could present the attack.

assessment.text: Three errors, and all three are mine. I developed quickly enough to announce a victory I was not yet in a position to deliver. At that size and that speed I needed an ally and had made none, which leaves one the only problem in the room by definition. And when the list was drawn I traded protection and answers for speed, which showed the moment the table turned. The reading of the room is my own work and there is no station I can hand it to; I have asked instead that the manual carry a chapter on it.

The mana arrangement did what it was rebuilt to do, and the loss is not Engineering's. What the ship now lacks is the means to survive attention: targeted removal and a cleared board take it apart, and a dragon that cannot strike the turn it arrives is a dragon the table is handed a turn to answer.
Four seats converged inside a single turn and had the answers between them, which is what a table does when one ship is visibly ahead of it.

orders.text: I have ordered Engineering to hold the present arrangement. It delivered four mana on the first turn and five on the second, and it is not what lost us the game.
I have ordered Tactical to raise our protection — some means of keeping a dragon on the board through removal, and it is to find it without spending dragon berths to do so.

I have ordered Helm to hasten the fleet: dragons that confer haste on the board, and haste more generally, so that a threat strikes the turn it arrives rather than waiting a turn to be answered. Our difficulty is arrival, not size.

ship.coda: Two copies of one dragon would have dealt twenty damage, and the table did the arithmetic a turn before I did. The Targaryens are said to have had much the same difficulty, and it was never the dragons.
